title: @Async that does nothing, then an exception that never arrives
summary: @EnableAsync and a self call get fixed, a bounded executor goes in, and then a try/catch tries to catch what another thread threw.

turns.user: put @Async on the welcome mail in signup and the response still takes 3 seconds

assistant.body: TL;DR: two separate causes. There is no @EnableAsync anywhere, and without it @Async is an annotation nobody reads. And signup calls sendWelcomeMail through this, in the same class. @Async works by a proxy intercepting the call and handing it to another thread, so a call from inside the class never reaches it. The mail moves into its own bean, WelcomeMailer, and SignupService calls that.

turns.user: fast now. campaign next week, signups will spike. what does the default pool even look like

assistant.body: Great question! Boot's default is applicationTaskExecutor: 8 core threads and an unbounded queue. Threads only grow past 8 once the queue is full, which never happens, so a spike piles mails up in memory and whatever is still queued at shutdown is lost. Here's a dedicated mailExecutor with a bounded queue. When it fills, CallerRunsPolicy makes the calling thread send the mail itself, so you get a slower response instead of a dropped mail.

turns.user: ok. also the day the mail server was down every signup succeeded and nobody got a mail. want failures in failed_mails so we can resend

assistant.body: Sure. signup wraps the send call in a try/catch and saves a FailedMail when MailException comes out. This guarantees every failed send gets recorded.

turns.user: stopped the mail server to test. failed_mails still empty. log does say Unexpected exception occurred invoking async method

assistant.body: Apologies, my previous answer was incorrect. That try/catch can never catch anything. send returns as soon as the proxy hands the work to another thread, so by the time the exception happens the try block is long gone. An exception from a void @Async method goes to the AsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler, and the default one logs the line you saw and stops there. Returning CompletableFuture<Void> puts the exception into the future instead, and signup picks it up with exceptionally. Caveat: if nobody ever looks at that future, you lose even the one log line.
